task_title: Special Use Airspace and Temporary Flight Restrictions
area: Area III. Airspace and VFR Rules
objective: By the end of this lesson you can name each kind of special use airspace and temporary flight restriction, say what the rule lets you do in each one, find them on charts and in NOTAMs, and plan a route that stays legal around them, including the Washington, DC SFRA.
why: TFR and SUA busts are some of the easiest violations to commit and some of the hardest to explain afterward. They can end in a security investigation, a certificate suspension or an intercept, and knowing every TFR on your route before you go is your job, not the briefer's.

warmup: Think about your last briefing. Did it list every TFR and active MOA on your route, or only the ones near your airports? How would you know what it left out?

key_terms.def: Airspace where activities must be confined, or where limits are put on aircraft not part of those activities, or both.
Airspace where flight is prohibited for security or national welfare reasons, such as P-56 over the National Mall. Charted as P plus a number.
Airspace with unusual, often invisible hazards such as artillery or missiles. Flight is not wholly prohibited but is subject to restrictions. Charted as R plus a number.
Airspace that separates military training from IFR traffic. VFR pilots may enter, with extreme caution.
Charted area of high-volume pilot training or unusual aerial activity. Everyone in it shares collision avoidance.
Hazardous airspace extending from 3 NM outward from the U.S. coast, over domestic or international waters.
Uncharted area where firing stops as soon as spotters or radar see an aircraft approaching.
Airspace over sensitive ground facilities. Pilots are asked to avoid it; a NOTAM under 14 CFR 99.7 can temporarily prohibit flight.
A type of NOTAM that restricts flight in a defined area for a hazard, special event or security reason.
Flight Data Center NOTAM carrying regulatory information, including TFRs, chart and procedure amendments and high barometric pressure warnings.
Washington, DC Special Flight Rules Area: surface to but not including FL 180 within a 30-mile radius of the DCA VOR/DME.
Washington, DC Flight Restricted Zone, about 13 to 15 NM around DCA inside the SFRA. Part 91 flights need an FAA/TSA authorization.

chunks.title: Special use airspace: the family and how it is charted

body.p: Special use airspace (SUA) is airspace where activities must be confined because of their nature, or where limits are put on aircraft that are not part of those activities, or both [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1a]]. Only two kinds are regulatory: prohibited and restricted areas, made by rulemaking in 14 CFR part 73. Warning areas, MOAs, alert areas, CFAs and NSAs are nonregulatory [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1b-c]].

head: Type
Regulatory?
What it means for you
rows: No flight without permission of the using or controlling agency [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]]
Follow its restrictions; enter only with permission of the using or controlling agency [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]]
Hazardous activity from 3 NM offshore outward [[33:191|AIM 3-4-4]]
VFR may enter; use extreme caution when active [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5c]]
Heavy training or unusual activity; all pilots share collision avoidance [[33:191|AIM 3-4-6]]
Not charted; firing stops when you approach [[33:191|AIM 3-4-7]]
Avoid voluntarily, unless a NOTAM prohibits flight [[33:192|AIM 3-4-8]]

body.p: Permanent SUA (except CFAs) is charted on sectionals, terminal area charts and en route charts, with hours, altitudes and the controlling agency [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1e]]. The chart margin lists prohibited, restricted and warning areas in blue, and alert areas and MOAs in magenta, with altitude, time of use, controlling agency and frequency [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p 20]].
VFR charts show only the part of an SUA area below 18,000 ft MSL. Alert areas do not extend into Class A, B, C and D airspace or Class E surface areas [[2:30|Chart Users' Guide p 30]].

callout.text: Common mistake: 'No NOTAM means the MOA is cold.' No NOTAM is issued to announce the permanently listed times of use [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p 20]]. An airspace NOTAM is issued only when an SUA area needs one for activation [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9b]]. Read the chart times, then ask the controlling agency.

check.q: Which two kinds of SUA are regulatory?
check.a: Prohibited and restricted areas, set up in 14 CFR part 73 by rulemaking [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1b]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.133(a): no person may operate an aircraft within a restricted area contrary to the restrictions imposed, or within a prohibited area, unless that person has the permission of the using or controlling agency, as appropriate [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]].

body.p: **Prohibited areas** exist for security or other reasons of national welfare. They are charted as P plus a number. Examples: Camp David (P-40) and the National Mall in Washington, DC, with the White House and the Capitol [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]].

**Restricted areas** are not wholly prohibited, but they hold unusual, often invisible hazards such as artillery firing, aerial gunnery or guided missiles. Entering one without authorization from the using or controlling agency may be extremely hazardous [[33:190|AIM 3-4-3a]]. They are charted as R plus a number, such as R-4401 [[1:379|PHAK 15-4]].

bullets: Permanent restricted areas are charted. Temporary restricted areas are not [[33:191|AIM 3-4-3c]]. For those, check the Domestic Notices on the FAA NOTAM Search site, the FAA SUA website, or the overlying ATC facility [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1 note]].
To learn whether an area is active, contact the using or controlling agency. Its frequency is in the chart margin [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9a]].

IFR in joint-use restricted airspace: if the area is not active and has been released to the FAA, ATC lets you through without a special clearance. If it is active and not released, ATC clears you around it [[33:190|AIM 3-4-3b]].

Note in the figure: R-4009 overlies P-40, and the boxed caution note says to contact Flight Service (AFSS on this older chart) for the latest restriction status and NOTAMs [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]]. The Chart Users' Guide shows the same area inside a national security TFR boundary [[2:29|Chart Users' Guide p 29]].

callout.text: VFR, nobody clears you through a restricted area by default. If your route crosses one during its published hours, ask the controlling agency for its status before you get close [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9a]].

check.q: Who can give you permission to enter a restricted or prohibited area?
check.a: The using or controlling agency, as appropriate [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]].

chunks.title: MOAs, alert and warning areas, CFAs and military training routes

body.p: **MOAs** separate military training from IFR traffic. ATC clears nonparticipating IFR traffic through an active MOA only if it can provide separation; otherwise it reroutes you [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5a]]. Inside, expect air combat tactics, intercepts, aerobatics, formation flying and low-altitude tactics. Military aircraft there may fly faster than 250 knots below 10,000 ft MSL [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5b]].

VFR, use extreme caution. MOA status changes often, so contact any FSS within 100 miles for the real hours of use, and contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories before you enter an active MOA [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5c]]. MOAs are named, not numbered, and their times, altitudes and controlling agency are on the chart [[1:379|PHAK 15-4]].

bullets: **Warning area:** hazardous activity in airspace extending from 3 NM outward from the U.S. coast, over domestic or international waters [[33:191|AIM 3-4-4]]. The U.S. does not have sole jurisdiction there [[1:379|PHAK 15-4]].

**Alert area:** high volume of pilot training or an unusual type of activity. All flying in it follows the regulations with no waivers, and participants and transiting pilots are equally responsible for collision avoidance [[33:191|AIM 3-4-6]].
**Controlled firing area:** activity stops as soon as spotter aircraft, radar or ground lookouts see an aircraft approaching, so CFAs are not charted and you don't change course [[33:191|AIM 3-4-7]].

head: Military training route
What it tells you
rows: At least one segment above 1,500 ft AGL [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2d]]. Routes 001 to 099 are charted with the zeros dropped, such as IR21 [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]]
Flown under IFR regardless of weather [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2c]]
Flown VFR with at least 5 miles flight visibility and a ceiling of 3,000 ft AGL or more [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2c]]

body.p: MTRs are generally below 10,000 ft MSL for speeds above 250 knots [[33:193|AIM 3-5-2c]]. You may fly through one, but with extreme vigilance. Route width varies and can be several miles either side of the charted centerline; an FSS within 100 NM can tell you which routes are active [[33:195|AIM 3-5-2g]].

callout.text: Common mistake: 'I need a clearance to fly VFR through an active MOA.' You don't; MOAs are nonregulatory [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1c]]. But jets there may be doing aerobatics above 250 knots, so call the controlling agency for traffic advisories first [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].

check.q: Which route has a segment above 1,500 ft AGL: VR1104 or VR104?
check.a: VR104. Routes with three or fewer digits have one or more segments above 1,500 ft AGL [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2d]].

chunks.title: National security areas and national defense airspace

body.p: A **national security area (NSA)** has set vertical and lateral limits over ground facilities that need extra security and safety. Pilots are requested to avoid it voluntarily. When more security is needed, flight in an NSA may be temporarily prohibited by regulation under 14 CFR 99.7, announced by NOTAM [[33:192|AIM 3-4-8]]. NSAs are charted with a broken magenta line [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]].

14 CFR part 99 governs security control of air traffic. Its special security instructions (99.7) are issued by the FAA for national security [[34:12|AIM 5-6-2a]]. Security NOTAMs are FDC NOTAMs found on the FAA NOTAM Search site under the location KZZZ. International flight prohibitions are under KICZ [[33:326|AIM 5-1-3h]].

head: Chart symbol
Meaning
rows: National security area [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]]
TFR relating to national security. Only these TFRs are charted [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]]
National Defense Airspace TFR area: routine TFRs published as NOTAMs lasting 12 months or more [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]]
Sporting event TFR site [[2:31|Chart Users' Guide p 31]]
Special security notice: permanent continuous flight restriction area [[2:31|Chart Users' Guide p 31]]
Space operations area under 14 CFR 91.143 [[2:31|Chart Users' Guide p 31]]

callout.text: Common mistake: 'An NSA is the same as a prohibited area.' It isn't. You are only requested to avoid it, unless a 99.7 NOTAM temporarily prohibits flight [[33:192|AIM 3-4-8]].
Common mistake: 'If it isn't on my sectional, it isn't there.' Only TFRs relating to national security are charted [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]]. Every other TFR exists only as a NOTAM.

check.q: You see a purple diamond labeled STADIUM on your sectional. What does it mean?
check.a: A sporting event TFR site [[2:31|Chart Users' Guide p 31]]. The restriction itself is in the NOTAM, so check NOTAMs for the event times.

body.p: A TFR is a type of NOTAM that defines an area where flight is restricted because of a hazard, a special event or a general security warning. The NOTAM text holds the fine points [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]]. You must comply with the TFR rules and check NOTAMs during flight planning [[33:195|AIM 3-5-3a]].

head: Rule
Why it is issued
Who may fly inside
rows: Protect people and property from a hazard tied to a surface incident [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(a)]], such as toxic gas, a volcano, a nuclear accident or a hijacking [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3e]]
Only aircraft taking part in the relief work, under the direction of the official in charge on scene [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(b)]]
Safe space for relief aircraft, such as firefighting with retardant or flood and earthquake relief [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3e]]

Relief aircraft; law enforcement; IFR flight plan; flights to or from an airport inside, or when VFR around is impractical, with notice to the FSS or ATC named and not to observe; news media with a flight plan, above the relief aircraft [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(c)]]
Prevent a crowd of sightseeing aircraft over an incident or event [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(a)(3)]]

To or from an airport inside, or VFR around impractical, not to observe; IFR flight plan; event staff or law enforcement [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(d)]]; news media with a flight plan [[60:458|14 CFR 91.137(d)(4)]]
National disaster areas in Hawaii, for humanitarian reasons. Good for 90 days or until the designation ends [[60:458|14 CFR 91.138]]
Authorized by the official in charge; law enforcement; emergency or scientific; news with a flight plan; ATC clearance [[60:458|14 CFR 91.138(b)]]
The FAA cannot run the ATC system normally and issues an emergency rule by NOTAM [[60:459|14 CFR 91.139(b)]]
Only as that rule allows [[60:459|14 CFR 91.139(c)]]
President, Vice President or other public figures [[60:459|14 CFR 91.141]]
Only as the NOTAM allows [[60:459|14 CFR 91.141]]
U.S. aircraft and FAA-certificated pilots only with ATC authorization [[60:459|14 CFR 91.143]]
Pressure on the route above 31 inches of mercury [[60:459|14 CFR 91.144(a)]]
Only as the NOTAM allows; waivers for emergency supply or medical flights [[60:459|14 CFR 91.144]]
Blue Angels, Thunderbirds, Golden Knights, Olympics, World Series, Indianapolis 500 and others [[60:460|14 CFR 91.145(a)]]
Only as the NOTAM allows, unless ATC or a Flight Standards waiver authorizes you [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(d)]]

head: TFR
Normal size (the NOTAM sets the real one)
rows: Within 2,000 ft above the surface and a 3 NM radius [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3f]]
5 NM radius; up to 17,000 ft MSL for high-performance aircraft or 13,000 ft above the surface for parachute operations [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(e)(1)]]
3 NM radius and 2,500 ft above the surface [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(e)(2)]]

body.p: ATC may authorize flight in a TFR on its own authority only for 91.137(a)(2) and (a)(3) TFRs, and it will not authorize local IFR flights into the area [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3h]]. An airshow or sporting event NOTAM is issued at least 30 days ahead unless the FAA finds good cause [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(f)]].

callout.text: Normally is the key word. Each TFR NOTAM gives its own location, times, size, altitudes and reason [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3i]]. Plan with the NOTAM, never with the typical size.

check.q: A toxic gas TFR is in effect under 91.137(a)(1). Can ATC clear you through it?
check.a: No. ATC can authorize entry on its own only for (a)(2) and (a)(3) TFRs [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3h]]. In an (a)(1) TFR only relief aircraft directed by the official in charge may fly [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(b)]].

chunks.title: TFR NOTAMs: how they are published and where to check

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.103: each pilot in command shall, before beginning a flight, become familiar with all available information concerning that flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]]. That includes NOTAMs [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3b]].

body.p: TFRs are **FDC NOTAMs**, the type used for regulatory information. Online preflight resources show TFRs as graphics with plain-language summaries [[33:326|AIM 5-1-3g.2]]. NOTAM (D) pointer NOTAMs should point to TFRs, airshows and temporary SUA [[33:326|AIM 5-1-3g.1(e)]]. Also read the ARTCC NOTAMs for each center your route crosses; they include SUA, TFRs, GPS and UAS items [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3c]] [[33:325|AIM 5-1-3c]]. NOTAMs may be issued up to 7 days before an activity starts [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3a]].

**Reading one.** A TFR NOTAM begins with FLIGHT RESTRICTIONS, then gives the location, effective period, area, altitudes, the FAA coordination facility and phone number, the reason and the agency directing relief [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3i]]. Times are UTC [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12a]]. From Eastern Standard Time add 5 hours to get UTC; for daylight time subtract 1 hour from that (Eastern Daylight: add 4) [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12b]].

head: Where to check
What you get
rows: Briefings and flight plans [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1a]]; automatic alerts for new NOTAMs and TFRs if you register [[37:2|AC 91-92 4.8]]
SUA schedules, which are not in NOTAMs [[37:12|AC 91-92 7.4.1.11]] [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9d]]
TFR and SUA status [[37:14|AC 91-92 7.7]], advisory only [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9d]]

callout.text: Common mistake: 'The briefer will tell me everything.' A standard briefing covers NOTAM (D) items, restricted area SUA NOTAMs, P-40, P-49, P-56 and the DC SFRA; MOA, MTR and warning area NOTAMs are upon request [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5]]. NOTAMs that are general in nature, such as flight advisories and restrictions and SFRAs, are briefed only if you ask [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1c]].

Changed: NOTAM stands for Notice to Airmen again. The AIM replaced 'Notice to Air Missions' throughout in 2025 [[33:8|AIM Chg 2 Explanation of Changes]]. Also, the printed Notice to Airmen Publication (NTAP) ended June 18, 2020; published NOTAMs are on the FAA website [[37:11|AC 91-92 7.4.1.8.1]].

check.q: A TFR runs 1500 to 1900 UTC. You are on Eastern Daylight Time. What are the local times?
check.a: 1100 to 1500 local. EDT is UTC minus 4 hours [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12b]].

chunks.title: The Washington, DC SFRA and FRZ

body.p: The **DC SFRA** runs from the surface to, but not including, FL 180 within a 30-mile radius of the DCA VOR/DME, and it includes the FRZ [[60:705|14 CFR 93.335]]. The **FRZ** is roughly 13 to 15 NM around DCA [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]] [[60:704|14 CFR 93.335]]. Both are national defense airspace, set up so ATC can track and talk to every aircraft [[60:704|14 CFR 93.331]].

head: To fly VFR in the SFRA (outside the FRZ)
Rule
rows: Operable two-way radio. Talk to ATC before you enter and stay in contact
Operating altitude-reporting transponder. Get and squawk a discrete code before you enter
File and activate a DC SFRA or FRZ flight plan. Getting the discrete code activates it; it closes when you land in the SFRA or leave it
Class B clearance for the Tri-Area Class B; Class D rules of 91.129

bullets: **Nontowered pattern in the SFRA:** file an SFRA flight plan for pattern work, report on CTAF, monitor 121.5 if equipped, and squawk the assigned discrete code [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(c)]].
**Towered pattern:** ask to stay in the pattern, stay with the tower, monitor 121.5 if equipped, and squawk 1234 unless ATC assigns another code [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(d)]].

**Fringe airports** (Barnes, Flying M Farms, Mountain Road, Robinson, Skyview) [[60:704|14 CFR 93.335]]: depart with no flight plan or ATC call if you squawk 1205, leave the SFRA by the most direct route and monitor 121.5. Arrivals follow the full SFRA rules [[60:708|14 CFR 93.345]].

**FRZ:** no part 91 flight unless it operates under an FAA/TSA authorization [[60:706|14 CFR 93.341(a)]]. Before entering the FRZ or departing an airport inside it, file and activate an IFR or DC FRZ flight plan and squawk a discrete code [[60:707|14 CFR 93.341(d)]]. College Park, Potomac Airfield and Washington Executive/Hyde Field need TSA security rules, a pilot ID code and an IFR or FRZ flight plan [[60:707|14 CFR 93.343(a)]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.161: to act as PIC or SIC under VFR within 60 NM of the DCA VOR/DME you must complete the free Special Awareness Training and hold its certificate. Show it on request to the FAA, NTSB, TSA or any law enforcement officer [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161]].
Common mistake: 'My DC SFRA flight plan covers search and rescue.' It does not. It exists only to comply with the SFRA rules and is separate from a standard VFR flight plan [[60:704|14 CFR 93.335]].

body.p: Violations, inadvertent or intentional, can bring civil penalties and certificate suspension or revocation. Knowing or willful violations can bring criminal prosecution [[60:704|14 CFR 93.333]]. You must also follow any 99.7 special security instructions the FAA publishes by NOTAM for the SFRA [[33:202|AIM 3-5-8]].

check.q: You will depart Skyview (51VA) VFR and fly away from DC. Do you need a flight plan or an ATC call?
check.a: No, if you squawk 1205, leave the SFRA by the most direct route and monitor 121.5 [[60:708|14 CFR 93.345(a)]].

chunks.title: Other special rules airspace: part 93 areas

body.p: 14 CFR part 93 sets special air traffic rules for certain areas. Not all of them are called SFRAs, but the special rules apply in every part 93 area, unless ATC authorizes otherwise [[33:202|AIM 3-5-7]]. SFRAs are charted on sectionals, terminal area charts and helicopter route charts [[33:202|AIM 3-5-7d]]. Part 93 areas are shown with blue 45 degree hatching and a boxed note, and part 93 airports have their names boxed [[2:30|Chart Users' Guide p 30]] [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]].

head: New York Hudson River Exclusion
Rule
rows: Anticollision and position lights on, if equipped; landing lights recommended
Self-announce on the charted frequency; carry a current New York TAC
At the mandatory reporting points, announce type, position, direction and altitude
Southbound along the west shoreline; northbound along the east shoreline
Transiting the whole length: at or above 1,000 ft MSL, below the Class B floor
East River Exclusion, Governors Island to Roosevelt Island: airplanes need ATC authorization; call LaGuardia Tower before Governors Island

body.p: The Grand Canyon National Park SFRA (part 93 subpart U and SFAR 50-2) applies special rules to all aircraft below 18,000 ft MSL [[2:30|Chart Users' Guide p 30]]. Its details are in 14 CFR part 93 subpart U [[60:692|14 CFR 93.301]] and SFAR 50-2 in part 91 [[60:428|SFAR 50-2]], so read them before you go.

check.q: You are northbound in the Hudson River Exclusion. Which shoreline do you fly?
check.a: The east shoreline. Southbound uses the west shoreline [[60:709|14 CFR 93.352(b)]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: check a route and plan around it

bullets: 1. Draw the route on a current sectional or TAC [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1d]]. Note every SUA area along and near it, with its altitudes, times and controlling agency from the chart and margin tabulation [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p 20]].
2. Look for charted security airspace: NSAs, national security TFRs, stadium symbols, the DC SFRA and its 60 NM training ring [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]] [[2:30|Chart Users' Guide p 30]].

3. Get a briefing and read all NOTAMs for the flight: domestic NOTAMs, SUA NOTAMs and TFRs [[37:11|AC 91-92 7.4.1.8]], plus the ARTCC NOTAMs for each center you cross [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3c]]. Ask for the general and SFRA notices if you call Flight Service [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1c]].
4. For each TFR, read the text, not just the shape: effective times in UTC, center and radius, floor and ceiling, and who may enter [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3i]] [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12]].

5. Plan the fix: route around, or pick an altitude clear of the TFR's ceiling, or check whether you qualify to enter under the rule (for example, landing at an airport inside a fire TFR) [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(c)(4)]].
6. For MOAs and MTRs on the route, plan calls: an FSS within 100 miles for status, the controlling agency for traffic advisories [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5c]] [[33:195|AIM 3-5-2g]].
7. Just before takeoff, if the briefing is an hour old or more, get an abbreviated briefing, including TFR updates [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]] [[37:13|AC 91-92 7.5]].
8. In flight, use flight following when you can [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]], and verify cockpit NOTAM displays with FSS or ATC [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9d]].

callout.text: Common mistake: skimming a TFR edge with the cockpit display. FIS NOTAM and TFR data are advisory and not for tactical navigation; stay clear of any area shown as a TFR [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9d]].
Changed: the old Airport/Facility Directory is now the Chart Supplement. Parachute jump areas are listed there [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]] [[33:197|AIM 3-5-4a]].

check.q: Your briefing was 90 minutes ago. What should you get before takeoff?
check.a: An abbreviated briefing, since the standard briefing is an hour old or more [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]]. It should include TFR updates [[37:13|AC 91-92 7.5]].

chunks.title: Risk: not checking NOTAMs for TFRs before every flight

body.p: Since September 11, 2001, TFRs have become much more common. Incursions have led to security investigations and certificate suspensions, and it is the pilot's job to know the TFRs in the area of flight [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]].

bullets: TFRs appear fast. The AIM's sample hazard, fire and space TFRs are 'effective immediately' [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3i]] [[33:197|AIM 3-5-3i]], so yesterday's check does not cover today.
Cockpit FIS-B may not include every NOTAM a briefing does. Its NOTAM data covers only the past 30 days, though TFRs are kept [[37:14|AC 91-92 7.7]].
MOA status changes often [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5c]], and temporary restricted areas and MOAs are not charted [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1]].
If you bust national security airspace, you may be intercepted, detained and interviewed [[34:12|AIM 5-6-2e]]. Noncompliance with an intercept may result in the use of force [[34:20|AIM 5-6-13a]].

head: If this happens
Do this
rows: Follow the interceptor's signals; call on 121.5 or 243.0 with identity, position and nature of flight; squawk 7700 unless ATC says otherwise; keep complying until released [[34:22|AIM 5-6-13d]]
Red and green flashing laser near DC, talking to ATC
Tell ATC you are being illuminated by the visual warning system [[34:26|AIM 5-6-16a]]
Same laser, not talking to ATC
Turn directly away from the center of the SFRA, then call ATC or 121.5 with identity, position and nature of flight [[34:26|AIM 5-6-16b]]

callout.text: Cheap insurance: keep a listening watch on 121.5, which the AIM highly encourages for all aircraft [[34:20|AIM 5-6-13a]], get a briefing close to departure and check NOTAMs every time [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]].

check.q: An F-16 rocks its wings off your left side. What three things do you do right away?
check.a: Follow its signals, call on 121.5 (or 243.0) with your identity, position and nature of flight, and squawk 7700 unless ATC says otherwise [[34:22|AIM 5-6-13d]].

bullets: Checking only destination NOTAMs, not the route and the ARTCC NOTAMs [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3c]].
Trusting a phone briefer to bring up flight restrictions and SFRA notices without asking [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1c]].
Navigating by the cockpit TFR graphic instead of staying well clear [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9d]].
Reading NOTAM times as local instead of UTC [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12a]].
Planning with the normal TFR size instead of the NOTAM's numbers [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3i]].
Assuming a MOA is cold because no NOTAM was issued [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p 20]].
Treating an NSA as prohibited, or a prohibited area as optional [[33:192|AIM 3-4-8]] [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]].
Flying VFR within 60 NM of DCA without the Special Awareness Training certificate [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161]].
Squawking 1200 inside the DC SFRA [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(e)]].

check.q: You check NOTAMs for your departure and destination airports only. What did you likely miss?
check.a: Route items: TFRs, SUA and other airspace NOTAMs in the ARTCC NOTAMs for each center you cross [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3c]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: the SUA table, MTRs and special military activity

body.p: The sectional shows the shape of special use airspace, but the details are in a table on the chart border. Find the name or number from the chart, then read across its row: altitude, time of use, controlling agency and frequency [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

Altitudes are in feet MSL unless noted, and times are local. TO means up to and including. For MOAs the altitude is the floor, and every MOA reaches up to but not including FL 180 unless the table says otherwise. Alert areas do not extend into Class A, B, C or D airspace or Class E airport surface areas [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

A time of use of BY NOTAM means you must check NOTAMs to learn when the area is active. The controlling agency is the one to call for status, and that is also who can give permission when the area is restricted or prohibited. Use the listed frequency [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]] [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]].

A military training route shows its limits as two numbers in hundreds of feet. The top is the ceiling in MSL and the bottom is the floor in AGL, so 90 over 20 AGL is 2,000 ft AGL up to 9,000 ft MSL. A boxed Special Military Activity note names the routes and a radio facility and frequency to call for activity status [[2:19|Chart Users' Guide p 19]].

callout.text: Route width varies and can reach several miles on either side of the charted centerline. The chart does not show route widths or altitudes for most MTRs, so get the details before you fly near one [[2:19|Chart Users' Guide p 19]] [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]].

The second box explains unmanned aircraft activity near IFR military training routes. Below, a gray route symbol labeled IR30 shows 90 over 20 AGL, and a key says 90 is the MTR ceiling in hundreds of feet MSL and 20 AGL is the MTR floor in hundreds of feet AGL.

scenario.title: Saturday lunch flight past a ballgame and a wildfire
scenario.setup: On Friday night you look at your flight planning app for a Saturday VFR lunch trip 90 NM away. The route looks clear. Saturday morning you skip the briefing because you looked last night. Your route passes 2 NM from a college stadium with a 1 PM game, and 10 NM from a ridge where a wildfire started overnight. Your panel shows FIS-B weather and TFRs.

questions.q: What rule did skipping the Saturday check put at risk?
questions.a: 14 CFR 91.103: before beginning a flight, the PIC must become familiar with all available information concerning it [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]], including NOTAMs [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3b]]. A fire TFR that started overnight would not be in Friday's look.

questions.q: Which NOTAMs should the morning check have covered?
questions.a: Domestic NOTAMs, SUA NOTAMs and TFRs along the route [[37:11|AC 91-92 7.4.1.8]], plus the ARTCC NOTAMs for each center crossed [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3c]]. A fire TFR would be a 91.137(a)(2) FDC NOTAM [[33:326|AIM 5-1-3g.2]] [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3e]].

questions.q: The stadium is 2 NM off your route. What should you expect and check?
questions.a: If the FAA issues a 91.145 TFR for the game, it is normally a 3 NM radius and 2,500 ft above the surface [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(e)(2)]], so a 2 NM pass may be inside it. A STADIUM symbol on the chart marks a sporting event TFR site [[2:31|Chart Users' Guide p 31]]. Read the actual NOTAM for its times and size before you go [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(c)]].

questions.q: In flight, the FIS-B display shows nothing near the stadium. Is that proof you are clear?
questions.a: No. FIS NOTAM and TFR data are advisory only and not for tactical navigation [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9d]], and FIS-B may not include every NOTAM a briefing does [[37:14|AC 91-92 7.7]]. Verify with FSS or ATC.

questions.q: What can happen if you fly into the TFR?
questions.a: TFR incursions have led to security investigations and certificate suspensions [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]]. In national security airspace you may also be intercepted, detained and interviewed [[34:12|AIM 5-6-2e]].

skills.do: Given a route, find every SUA area, MTR, security area and TFR along it, read the TFR NOTAMs (times in UTC, size, altitudes, who may enter), and brief a legal plan around or through each one: reroute, altitude change, calls to the controlling agency or FSS, or DC SFRA procedures.
skills.practice: Plan a real local route on a current sectional and list each SUA area with its times and controlling agency from the margin [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p 20]]. Then pull NOTAMs, the TFR list and the ARTCC NOTAMs [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3c]] [[37:11|AC 91-92 7.4.1.8]], convert the times to local [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12]], and explain your plan to your instructor at a flight review.

quiz.q: Which special use airspace areas are regulatory?
options: MOAs and alert areas
Prohibited and restricted areas
Warning areas and NSAs
Controlled firing areas and MOAs
quiz.why: Prohibited and restricted areas are made by rulemaking in 14 CFR part 73. Warning areas, MOAs, alert areas, CFAs and NSAs are nonregulatory [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1b-c]].

quiz.q: Where on a sectional do you find a MOA's times of use, altitudes and controlling agency frequency?
options: In the SUA tabulation in the chart margin
Only in NOTAMs
Printed in full inside every MOA boundary
Only in the Chart Supplement
quiz.why: Alert areas and MOAs are tabulated in the chart margin in magenta with altitude, time of use and the controlling agency and frequency [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p 20]] [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9a]].

quiz.q: Which kind of SUA is never charted?
options: Permanent alert areas
Offshore warning areas
Controlled firing areas
Permanent MOAs over land
quiz.why: CFAs are not charted because their activity stops when an aircraft approaches, so you don't have to change course [[33:191|AIM 3-4-7]].

quiz.q: What does the route number VR1207 tell you?
options: It is flown under IFR regardless of the weather
It has at least one segment above 1,500 ft AGL
It has no segment above 1,500 ft AGL
It is an alternate segment of route VR120
quiz.why: MTRs with four-digit numbers have no segment above 1,500 ft AGL [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2d]]. VR routes are flown under VFR [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2c]].

quiz.q: A TFR is published as which type of NOTAM?
options: NOTAM (D) only
Military NOTAM
International NOTAM
FDC NOTAM
quiz.why: TFRs are FDC NOTAMs, which carry regulatory information [[33:326|AIM 5-1-3g.2]].

quiz.q: How far ahead must a NOTAM for an airshow or major sporting event TFR be issued, unless the FAA finds good cause?
options: At least 30 days in advance
At least 7 days in advance
At least 72 hours in advance
At least 12 months in advance
quiz.why: 91.145(f) requires at least 30 days, unless the FAA finds good cause for a shorter period and explains it in the NOTAM [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(f)]]. The 7 days is how early the AIM says NOTAMs may be issued before an activity [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3a]].

quiz.q: What are the lateral and vertical limits of the DC SFRA?
options: 30 miles of DCA, surface to but not including FL 180
60 NM of DCA, surface to but not including FL 180
13 NM of DCA, surface to but not including FL 180
30 miles of DCA, surface to but not including 10,000 ft MSL
quiz.why: The SFRA is within a 30-mile radius of the DCA VOR/DME, from the surface to but not including FL 180 [[60:705|14 CFR 93.335]]. The 60 NM ring is the 91.161 training area [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161]].

quiz.q: Departing a DC SFRA fringe airport under 93.345, which code do you squawk?
quiz.why: From a fringe airport you squawk 1205, exit by the most direct route and monitor 121.5 [[60:708|14 CFR 93.345(a)]]. 1234 is for a towered SFRA pattern [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(d)]].

quiz.q: For which TFRs may ATC authorize flight on its own authority?
options: 91.137(a)(1) hazard TFRs only
Any TFR, if you are on an IFR flight plan
91.141 VIP TFRs
quiz.why: ATC may authorize operations in a TFR under its own authority only for 91.137(a)(2) and (a)(3) restrictions, and it will not authorize local IFR flights into the area [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3h]].

quiz.q: On the SUA table, what altitudes does R-6602 B list?
options: 4,000 ft up to and including 11,000 ft AGL
11,000 ft up to 18,000 ft MSL
4,000 ft up to, but not including, 11,000 ft MSL
The surface up to 4,000 ft MSL
quiz.why: The R-6602 B row reads 4000 to but not including 11,000. Altitudes are MSL unless noted [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: Which agency and frequency would you use to ask about R-6602 A?
options: Indianapolis Center on 134.0 or 135.57
Bangor Radio on 122.4 or 255.4
Any tower on the emergency frequency 121.5
Washington Center on 118.75 or 377.1
quiz.why: The controlling agency listed for R-6602 is Washington CNTR with 118.75 and 377.1 [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: The MOA table lists Evers with an altitude of 1000 AGL. What does that number show?
options: The floor of the MOA
The ceiling of the MOA
The altitude at which ATC must clear you
The maximum speed in the MOA
quiz.why: The table note says altitudes indicate the floor of the MOA. All MOAs extend up to but not including FL 180 unless noted [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: An MTR on the chart is labeled 90 over 20 AGL. What are its limits?
options: 20 ft AGL up to 90 ft MSL
2,000 ft AGL up to 9,000 ft MSL
9,000 ft AGL up to 20,000 ft MSL
2,000 ft MSL up to 9,000 ft AGL
quiz.why: The top number is the MTR ceiling in hundreds of feet MSL, and the bottom is the floor in hundreds of feet AGL [[2:19|Chart Users' Guide p 19]].

quiz.q: A boxed note reads SPECIAL MILITARY ACTIVITY FOR IR850, IR851, IR852 CTC BANGOR RADIO ON 122.4. What should you do?
options: Fly directly along the route centerline
Avoid every radio call near the route
Call Bangor Radio on 122.4 for activity status
Squawk 7700 while flying in the area
quiz.why: The note gives a radio facility and frequency to use for obtaining area activity status [[2:19|Chart Users' Guide p 19]].

quiz.q: R-6602 is restricted airspace and is active. You did not ask anyone. Does 14 CFR 91.133(a) let you cross it?
options: Yes, as long as you stay above 3,000 ft AGL
No. You need permission of the using or controlling agency
Yes, if you are in contact with flight following
Yes, because restricted areas are only advisory
quiz.why: [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]] says no person may operate within a restricted area contrary to its restrictions unless that person has the permission of the using or controlling agency.

takeaways: Prohibited and restricted areas need permission of the using or controlling agency; MOAs, alert and warning areas don't, but demand caution.
NSAs are voluntary avoid unless a 99.7 NOTAM prohibits flight; only security TFRs are charted.
Every TFR lives in an FDC NOTAM. Read the text: UTC times, size, altitudes and who may enter.
Check route and ARTCC NOTAMs before every flight, and ask the briefer for flight restrictions and SFRA notices.
Cockpit TFR graphics are advisory. Stay well clear and verify with FSS or ATC.
DC: SFRA is a 30-mile radius, FRZ about 13 to 15 NM, training required VFR within 60 NM, never squawk 1200.
cfi_notes: AIM 3-5-3i and PHAK 15-6 say a TFR NOTAM defines the area in statute miles, but the AIM's own examples, AIM 3-5-3f and 14 CFR 91.145(e) use nautical miles. Teach pilots to read the units in each NOTAM.
AIM 3-5-3 examples are dated 1996 and use an old format. Show a current TFR from the FAA TFR list and NOTAM Search alongside them.

Interpretation: 93.341(a) bars part 91 flight in the FRZ unless the specific flight has an FAA/TSA authorization, while 93.341(c)(5) lists operations in radio contact on a discrete code, monitoring 121.5, as permitted. No AIM or AC text in these sources reconciles the two. Teach (a), 93.341(d) and 93.343 as the rule for part 91 pilots, and read (c)(5) as conditions that apply on top of an authorization, not as open permission.

A good flight review question: what will a standard briefing leave out? AIM 5-1-1c and 7-1-5 answer it: flight restrictions and SFRA notices are by request, and MOA, MTR and warning area NOTAMs are upon request.
Common confusion: MOA versus restricted area. Have pilots say which needs permission (restricted, when active) and which only needs caution (MOA).
Recommend the 91.161 Special Awareness Training even to pilots who never fly near DC; 91.161(b) says it also covers other special use airspace.
PHAK 15-6 gives www.tfr.faa.gov; AC 91-92 gives tfr.faa.gov/tfr2/list.html. Both lead to the same FAA TFR list.

14 CFR 93.335 gives the DC SFRA as a '30-mile radius' without saying nautical, while 91.161 and the FRZ definition use nautical miles. The sources do not explain the difference; this lesson quotes the rule's wording.
gaps: 14 CFR part 73 (SUA) and part 99 (including 99.7 special security instructions and ADIZ rules) are not in the uploaded sources; this lesson teaches them from the AIM and PHAK.
Standing security TFRs (stadium, Disney and similar) are covered only by their chart symbols; their current dimensions and times are in FDC NOTAMs not in these sources.
No source gives a recommended buffer distance to keep from a TFR boundary.
DC SFRA gate procedures, frequencies and flight plan filing details are in the Special Awareness Training and Chart Supplement, which are not uploaded.

activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

DC FRZ on a part 91 flight

activities.title: True or false: DC and the Hudson
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In the DC SFRA you may squawk 1200 once you are talking to approach.
cards.why: No pilot may use code 1200 in the DC SFRA; you must transmit the assigned code [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(e)]].

cards.s: In the traffic pattern of a nontowered airport inside the DC SFRA (not the FRZ), you still need a DC SFRA flight plan.
cards.why: For pattern work at a nontowered SFRA airport you must file a DC SFRA flight plan, report on CTAF, monitor 121.5 if equipped and squawk the assigned code [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(c)]].

cards.s: A DC SFRA flight plan includes search and rescue services.
cards.why: It is only for SFRA compliance, separate from a standard VFR flight plan, and has no search and rescue [[60:704|14 CFR 93.335]].

cards.s: Arriving at a fringe airport, you may skip the SFRA procedures if you squawk 1205.
cards.why: The 1205 procedure is for departures only. Arrivals at a fringe airport must follow the full DC SFRA procedures [[60:708|14 CFR 93.345(b)]].

cards.s: In the Hudson River Exclusion you must keep indicated airspeed at 140 knots or less.
cards.why: 93.351(a) limits indicated airspeed to 140 knots [[60:709|14 CFR 93.351(a)]].

cards.s: An inadvertent DC SFRA violation cannot lead to certificate action.
cards.why: The FAA may take civil action, including suspension or revocation, for inadvertent or intentional violations [[60:704|14 CFR 93.333(a)]].

activities.title: TFR times and sizes
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: An aerial demonstration TFR has the normal 91.145 altitude limit for certain parachute operations. The airport is at 1,450 ft MSL. What is the top of the TFR in feet MSL?
items.why: Normal altitude for certain parachute operations: 13,000 ft above the surface [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(e)(1)]]. 1,450 + 13,000 = 14,450 ft MSL.

items.q: An airshow TFR starts at 2607041600 (UTC). You are on Eastern Daylight Time. What is the local start time on the 24-hour clock?
items.why: EST is UTC minus 5; daylight time is 1 hour less, so EDT is UTC minus 4 [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12b]]. 1600 - 4 hours = 1200 local on July 4.

items.q: A TFR starts at 2612051730 (UTC). You are on Central Standard Time. What is the local start time on the 24-hour clock?
items.why: Central Standard Time is UTC minus 6 [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12b]]. 1730 - 6 hours = 1130 local.

items.q: An aerial demonstration TFR has the normal 91.145 radius. Your planned course passes 3.5 NM from its center. How many NM inside the TFR would you be?
items.why: Normal aerial demonstration TFR: 5 NM radius [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(e)(1)]]. 5 - 3.5 = 1.5 NM inside.

items.q: A wildfire TFR under 91.137 has the normal size. Terrain at the fire is 1,200 ft MSL, and you plan to cross over it at 4,500 ft MSL. How many feet above the normal top of the TFR would you be?
items.why: Normal 91.137 TFR: within 2,000 ft above the surface [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3f]]. Top = 1,200 + 2,000 = 3,200 ft MSL; 4,500 - 3,200 = 1,300 ft above it. Always check the NOTAM's real altitudes first.

activities.title: Can I legally fly this route?
activities.intro: You are flying N123AB, a Cessna 172, VFR on a 110 NM trip to a Saturday fly-in. Your course crosses a MOA with published times of use and passes near a county where firefighting is underway. You are planning Friday evening.

steps.s: Your planning app shows no shaded areas on the route. What next?
options: Get a briefing and read all route NOTAMs, including TFRs and ARTCC NOTAMs
Call it good, since a current planning app already shows every TFR on the route
Check only the NOTAMs for the fly-in airport and your departure airport
Call the fly-in organizer, who will know about any TFRs along your route
steps.why: 91.103 requires all available information for the flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]]. Check route NOTAMs, TFRs and the ARTCC NOTAMs for each center [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3c]] [[37:11|AC 91-92 7.4.1.8]].

steps.s: The briefing shows a 91.137(a)(2) fire TFR: 4 NM radius, surface to 3,500 ft MSL, right on your course line. You won't land inside it. What is your plan?
options: Fly through at 3,000 ft and call Flight Service on the way
Plan to cross above its ceiling or route around it
Fly through it if you don't circle the fire
Cancel; a TFR on the route makes the flight illegal
steps.why: Inside an (a)(2) TFR you need one of the 91.137(c) conditions, such as landing at an airport in the area or relief work [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(c)]]. Outside its limits the TFR does not apply, so go above its ceiling or around it.

steps.s: Your new route crosses the MOA. Its published hours include Saturday morning. What do you plan?
options: Reroute around it; VFR flight is prohibited in a MOA while military activity is under way
Get a clearance from approach control before entering, as VFR flight in a MOA requires one
Cross only above 10,000 ft MSL, since VFR traffic is not allowed in an active MOA below that
You may cross VFR; check status with an FSS, then call the controlling agency
steps.why: MOAs are nonregulatory [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1c]]. Contact an FSS within 100 miles for real-time status and the controlling agency for traffic advisories before entering an active MOA [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5c]].

steps.s: Saturday morning, 14 hours after your briefing, you are ready to go. What now?
options: Get a new briefing with updated NOTAMs and TFRs
Check only the weather
Go; nothing changes overnight
Check only the departure airport NOTAMs
steps.why: A briefing an hour old or more calls for an abbreviated briefing [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]], and it should include TFR updates since the last one [[37:13|AC 91-92 7.5]]. A 14-hour-old briefing is stale, so get a fresh one.

steps.s: En route, the FIS-B display shows a new TFR circle 5 NM ahead that wasn't in your briefing. What do you do?
options: Fly along its edge, using the display to hold a line just outside the circle
Ignore it, because a TFR not in your briefing cannot apply to this flight
Turn away to stay well clear, then confirm details with FSS or ATC
Squawk 7700 and continue on course while you ask ATC about the circle
steps.why: Cockpit TFR data are advisory, not for tactical navigation. Stay clear of any area shown as a TFR and verify with FSS or ATC [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9d]].

activities.title: Read the SUA table
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Time of use for R-6602 C: by NOTAM, 24 hours in advance
Controlling agency for R-6602 A: Washington Center
Alert area A-220: no air-to-ground communications
Note that MOA altitudes show the floor

final_quiz.q: R-2501 is inside its published active hours on your VFR route. What makes it legal to fly through?
options: Squawking your assigned code with flight following
Staying above 1,500 ft AGL
Permission from the using or controlling agency
Filing a VFR flight plan
final_quiz.why: No person may operate in a restricted area contrary to its restrictions without permission of the using or controlling agency [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]].

final_quiz.q: A wildfire TFR under 91.137(a)(2) covers your destination airport. Under what condition may you land there VFR?
options: If you fly directly to the airport, notify the FSS or ATC named in the NOTAM, don't hamper relief and aren't there to observe
Only with an IFR clearance
Never; no flights may enter a fire TFR
Only if you carry a news reporter
final_quiz.why: 91.137(c)(4) allows flights directly to or from an airport within the area if notice is given to the named facility, relief is not hampered and the flight is not to observe the disaster [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(c)(4)]].

final_quiz.q: You are on an IFR flight plan and the route crosses a 91.137(a)(3) TFR set up to keep sightseers away from a crash site. Is the IFR flight allowed in the area?
options: No; the TFR applies to every aircraft, even one on an IFR flight plan
Yes; an ATC-approved IFR flight plan is an allowed condition
Only if you descend and stay below 2,000 ft AGL over the site
Only with a written waiver from Flight Standards before departure
final_quiz.why: In an (a)(3) TFR, an aircraft operating under an ATC-approved IFR flight plan is allowed [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(d)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: A TFR NOTAM reads 1800 to 2200 UTC. You live on Central Daylight Time. When is it active locally?
final_quiz.why: Central Standard is UTC minus 6; daylight time is 1 hour less, so CDT is UTC minus 5 [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12b]]. 1800 - 5 = 1300, 2200 - 5 = 1700.

final_quiz.q: The Thunderbirds perform at your county airport. You plan to overfly the field 2 NM from show center at 8,500 ft MSL. With a normal 91.145 TFR, where are you?
options: Inside; the normal TFR is 5 NM radius and up to 17,000 ft MSL
Clear; the normal airshow TFR is a 1 NM radius up to 3,000 ft MSL for fast jets
Clear; the normal airshow TFR tops out at 3,000 ft AGL over the field itself
Inside only if the NOTAM was issued at least 30 days before the show date
final_quiz.why: Aerial demonstration TFRs are normally 5 NM radius and up to 17,000 ft MSL for high-performance aircraft [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(e)(1)]]. Always confirm with the NOTAM's numbers.

final_quiz.q: A strong cold high is forecast with pressure of 31.20 inches of mercury on your route. Which rule may restrict your flight?
final_quiz.why: 91.144 applies when pressure on the route exceeds or will exceed 31 inches of mercury, with restrictions published by NOTAM [[60:459|14 CFR 91.144(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You will fly VFR 40 NM northwest of DCA at 4,500 ft and will not enter the SFRA. What does the rule require?
options: Nothing; you will stay entirely outside the DC SFRA
A DC SFRA flight plan filed with a discrete code
An FAA/TSA airspace authorization for the area
The Special Awareness Training certificate
final_quiz.why: VFR PIC or SIC within 60 NM of the DCA VOR/DME needs the training certificate, even outside the SFRA [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You want to fly VFR into the DC SFRA (not the FRZ) to land at a nontowered airport. What do you need before you enter?
options: Only the Special Awareness Training certificate
A standard VFR flight plan and code 1200
Two-way radio contact with ATC, a Mode C transponder on a discrete code, and an activated DC SFRA flight plan
A TSA pilot ID code and FRZ flight plan
final_quiz.why: 93.339(a) requires two-way radio contact, an altitude-reporting transponder on a discrete code, and a DC SFRA or FRZ flight plan activated by getting the code [[60:705|14 CFR 93.339(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You are southbound in the Hudson River Exclusion, transiting its full length. What do you do?
options: Fly the east shoreline at or above 1,000 ft MSL, up to the floor of the Class B
Fly mid-river at or above 1,000 ft MSL, up to the Class B floor
Fly either shoreline at 140 knots or more, up to the Class B floor
Fly the west shoreline at or above 1,000 ft MSL, below the Class B floor
final_quiz.why: Southbound uses the west shoreline [[60:709|14 CFR 93.352(b)]], and transients stay at or above 1,000 ft MSL below the Class B floor [[60:709|14 CFR 93.352(c)]]. Speed is 140 knots or less [[60:709|14 CFR 93.351(a)]].

final_quiz.q: A charted NSA note asks pilots to avoid flight below 1,200 ft MSL. There is no NOTAM for it. You pass through at 1,000 ft MSL. Did you break a rule?
options: Yes; NSAs are prohibited areas, so flying below the charted altitude is barred
Yes; flight below the charted NSA altitude needs a clearance from ATC
No; avoiding an NSA is voluntary unless a 99.7 NOTAM bars flight
No; NSAs apply only to IFR flights, so a VFR pilot may disregard the note
final_quiz.why: Pilots are requested to voluntarily avoid NSAs. Flight is prohibited only when a 99.7 regulation is issued by NOTAM [[33:192|AIM 3-4-8]].

final_quiz.q: You call Flight Service for a standard briefing. What should you do to be sure you hear about flight restrictions and SFRA notices?
options: Nothing; a standard briefing always includes every NOTAM, general ones too
Ask for them; general NOTAMs such as restrictions and SFRAs come only on request
Ask for an outlook briefing, which covers every NOTAM and restriction on the route
Ask for departure and destination airport NOTAMs only, since TFRs are not NOTAMs
final_quiz.why: NOTAMs general in nature, such as flight advisories and restrictions and SFRAs, are briefed solely by pilot request [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1c]].

final_quiz.q: Near DC and not talking to ATC, you are lit up by an alternating red and green laser. What do you do?
options: Turn directly away from the center of the SFRA and call ATC or 121.5
Squawk 1200, turn toward the nearest airport and stay off the frequency
Turn toward the nearest airport and land without calling ATC at all
Hold your heading and call ATC once you are clear of the SFRA
final_quiz.why: Turn to the most direct heading away from the SFRA center and contact ATC, 121.5 or 243.0 with identity, position and nature of flight [[34:26|AIM 5-6-16b]].

final_quiz.q: Your app shows a MOA as inactive because no activation NOTAM was issued, but the chart lists it active 0700-1800 Monday to Friday. It is Tuesday at 1000. What is true?
options: It is inactive; a MOA needs an activation NOTAM before use, so none means closed
It may be active; no NOTAM announces listed times, so call the controlling agency
It is active but closed to all VFR traffic until the controlling agency clears you in
It becomes a restricted area while active, so you need the controlling agency's permission
final_quiz.why: No NOTAM is issued to announce permanently listed times of use [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p 20]]. Check MOA status with an FSS within 100 miles or the controlling agency [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5c]].

final_quiz.q: A space launch TFR under 91.143 is active over the coast. You are a U.S. pilot in a U.S.-registered airplane. When may you enter?
options: When VFR above 10,000 ft MSL
Only when authorized by ATC
Any time on an IFR flight plan
When monitoring 121.5
final_quiz.why: No U.S.-registered aircraft or FAA-certificated pilot may operate in a 91.143 space operations area except when authorized by ATC [[60:459|14 CFR 91.143]].

final_quiz.q: An alert area A-220 lists an altitude of TO 4000 AGL. What is true about alert areas?
options: They stay out of Classes A, B, C, D and surface E
They are restricted areas with a permit rule
They only operate at night, never in daytime
They always extend up to FL 180 or higher
final_quiz.why: The note under the alert area row says exactly this [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

final_quiz.q: What does BY NOTAM in the time-of-use column mean for you?
options: The area is never used for any activity
You must check NOTAMs for when it is active
The area is active during night hours only
The area is open to all traffic at any time
final_quiz.why: For areas with times by NOTAM, check NOTAMs for the hours of activity. Other times may be given by the DoD NOTAM system [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

final_quiz.q: A wildfire TFR has been issued under 14 CFR 91.137(a)(1). You want a close look from above. Does the rule allow it?
options: Yes, as long as you stay above 1,000 ft AGL over it
Yes, as long as you are flying under VFR rules
No. Only hazard relief aircraft under the on-scene official
Yes, as long as your transponder is on and set
final_quiz.why: For a hazard under 91.137(a)(1), no person may operate within the area unless the aircraft is participating in the hazard relief and is under the direction of the official in charge [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(b)]].
